name: AEGIS-128X2 / AEGIS-128X4 / AEGIS-256X2 / AEGIS-256X4 (parallel AEGIS modes, libaegis)
workload: Single-core AEAD encryption throughput on 16 KB messages, comparing AEGIS-128L/256 and their X2/X4 parallel modes against OpenSSL's AES-GCM on Intel Raptor Lake (i9-13900K), AMD EPYC 7543, and AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen4, VAES/AVX-512).
claimed_speedup: AEGIS-128X2: 318 Gbps vs AES128-GCM 81 Gbps on i9-13900K (~3.9x); AEGIS-128X4: 348 Gbps vs AES128-GCM 94 Gbps on Ryzen 7 7700 (~3.7x); AEGIS-256X4: 277 Gbps vs AES256-GCM 81 Gbps on Ryzen 7 7700 (~3.4x); even plain AEGIS-128L: 190 Gbps vs 81 Gbps on i9-13900K (~2.3x)
compiler_and_flags: AEGIS reference implementation in Zig (from the IETF AEGIS specification's reference code); baseline is OpenSSL 3.1.0 / 3.1.1 AES-GCM. Exact compiler/build flags for the OpenSSL side are not stated in the paper.
hardware: Intel Core i9-13900K (Raptor Lake); AMD EPYC 7543; AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen4, AVX-512+VAES) — single core, 16 KB messages
stars_or_usage: 146 stars (aegis-aead/libaegis); is the reference implementation cited by the IETF AEGIS draft/RFC
tradeoffs: The X2/X4 speedups require VAES/AVX-512 or equivalent wide vector-AES instructions; on CPUs without vector-AES, plain AEGIS-128L/256 is as fast or faster than the X-variants. AEGIS has a shorter cryptanalytic track record than AES-GCM (in active study since 2013).
caveats: Benchmark is single-core and only shown for 16 KB messages in the cited tables (short-message behavior is discussed qualitatively, not tabulated here). Compiler/flags for the OpenSSL baseline build are unstated, so Tier A rests on the CPU models and public reference code being explicit. Independent corroboration: eBACS/SUPERCOP's CAESAR benchmark page shows aegis128l at ~0.24 cycles/byte vs a SUPERCOP AES-GCM reference (aes128gcmv1) at ~0.95 cycles/byte on a 2024 Intel Core 5 210H (https://bench.cr.yp.to/results-caesar/amd64-freshwrap,big.html) — that reference AES-GCM implementation is not confirmed to be OpenSSL's, so it is not used as the primary evidence here.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos aead cipher c++ (surfaced aegis-aead/libaegis); corroborated via bench.cr.yp.to/results-aead/amd64-hertz.html
IACR ePrint search q=AEGIS: https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/523 'Adding more parallelism to the AEGIS authenticated encryption algorithms'

name: HiAE (High-throughput Authenticated Encryption)
workload: Single-core AEAD encrypt+authenticate throughput across 14 named ARM and x86 CPUs (server/desktop/laptop/mobile/router), message sizes 64B-16384B, -O3 builds, vs OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM, AES-256-CTR, SNOW-V-GCM, Rocca, Rocca-S and AEGIS-128L.
claimed_speedup: 16 KB AEAD: 340.02 Gbps (HiAE) vs 51.90 Gbps (AES-256-GCM) on AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (~6.5x); 171.46 Gbps vs 36.49 Gbps on Intel Xeon W9-3495X (~4.7x); 253.19 Gbps vs 38.80 Gbps on AMD EPYC 9334 (~6.5x); paper states HiAE exceeds 340 Gbps on x86 and 180 Gbps on ARM, calling it the fastest measured AEAD on ARM
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.4 (x86 servers/desktop, Ubuntu 22.04 or WSL2), GCC 10.3 (Kunpeng/openEuler), GCC 14 (Apple M-series), ArkCompiler 3.0.0.5 (Huawei mobile), openWRT GCC 11.2.0 (router); -O3 maximum optimization used for every implementation compared
hardware: 14 named CPUs incl. Intel Xeon W9-3495X, AMD EPYC 9334, AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, Intel Xeon Gold 6326/6242R, Intel Core i7-11700, Intel Xeon E5-2620 v3, HiSilicon Kunpeng 920/920X, Kirin 9000S, Qualcomm Snapdragon 8+ Gen1, Apple M1/M2 Max/M3 Pro, Rockchip RK3568
tradeoffs: Reference repo carries no LICENSE file, so the code can be studied but not safely reused/redistributed as-is. HiAE is a brand-new (2025) design with far less cryptanalysis history than AES-GCM or even AEGIS; the paper's own results show HiAE falls slightly behind Rocca on older Xeon Gold 6242R/E5-2620 v3 CPUs that lack VAES.
caveats: Very new design (2025), under active cryptanalysis (see follow-up IACR ePrint papers 2025/1180 'Cryptanalysis of the Authenticated Stream Cipher HiAE', 2025/1203, and 2025/1235 rebutting a claimed attack). No open-source license on the reference implementation.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=HiAE: https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/377 'HiAE: A High-Throughput Authenticated Encryption Algorithm for Cross-Platform Efficiency'

name: SNOW-V-GCM
workload: Single-thread AEAD encryption throughput vs input size (64B-16384B) on a laptop CPU; SNOW-V-GCM implemented in C++ with AVX2/AES-NI/PCLMULQDQ intrinsics, benchmarked using code extracted from OpenSSL's own benchmarking harness against OpenSSL 3.0.0-dev (2019-04-01) AES-256-GCM assembly.
claimed_speedup: 16384B: 38.91 Gbps (SNOW-V-GCM) vs 34.42 Gbps (AES-256-GCM asm), ~13% faster. Advantage shrinks with message size and reverses below ~2048B (e.g. at 64B, AES-256-GCM wins: 8.54 Gbps vs 5.16 Gbps).
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 + NASM, 'most possible optimizations switched on', native x64 build
hardware: Intel Core i7-8650U @1.90GHz (Turbo up to 4.20GHz), single thread
stars_or_usage: SNOW-V is a 3GPP/ETSI candidate stream cipher for 5G; no widely used, independently maintained open-source repo of SNOW-V-GCM was located in this search
tradeoffs: Only faster than OpenSSL AES-256-GCM for larger messages (roughly >=4KB); for short messages (<2KB) OpenSSL's hand-tuned, instruction-stitched assembly wins outright. The paper's own C++ implementation does not get GHASH "for free" the way OpenSSL's asm does.
caveats: Benchmarked on a single, now-old (2018-era) ultrabook CPU against a pre-release OpenSSL snapshot (3.0.0-dev); no maintained public repo found, so usability is 'reference' rather than 'copyable' even though full source is printed in the paper's appendix.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=SNOW-V: https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/1143 'A new SNOW stream cipher called SNOW-V'

name: Bitsliced AEGIS-128L / AEGIS-128X2 (constant-time, no-AES-NI platforms)
workload: Single-core, 16 KB message AEAD encrypt+authenticate throughput on ARM/RISC-V CPUs lacking AES instructions and on WebAssembly, plus ARM Cortex-M4 cycle counts, vs side-channel-protected (bitsliced) AES-128-GCM from OpenSSL 3.3 (on Cortex-A53) and BoringSSL (elsewhere); also a pure-TypeScript benchmark on Apple M5 Max/Bun vs the noble-ciphers pure-JS AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305.
claimed_speedup: ARM Cortex-A53: 423 Mb/s (AEGIS-128L) vs 261 Mb/s (protected AES-GCM), ~1.6x; WebAssembly on Apple M1 host: 2912 Mb/s (AEGIS-128X2) vs 480 Mb/s (protected AES-GCM), ~6.1x; SpacemiT X60 RISC-V: 333 Mb/s vs 137 Mb/s, ~2.4x; Cortex-M4: 185 cycles/byte (bitsliced AEGIS-128L) vs 246 c/B protected / 208 c/B unprotected AES-128-GCM; pure-JS on Apple M5 Max at 1 MB: 324 MB/s (AEGIS-128L) vs 182 MB/s (AES-128-GCM, ~1.8x) and 256 MB/s (ChaCha20-Poly1305, ~1.3x)
hardware: ARM Cortex-A53 (64-bit); SpacemiT X60 (RISC-V, no AES ext.); SiFive U74 (RISC-V, no AES ext.); WebAssembly on an Apple M1 host; ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller; Apple M5 Max (pure TypeScript under Bun)
stars_or_usage: 9 stars (aegis-aead/aegis-bitsliced); companion pure-TypeScript port jedisct1/js-aegis-aead (MIT, 4 stars) used for the JS numbers
tradeoffs: Purpose-built for platforms lacking AES/vector-AES instructions (microcontrollers, RISC-V without crypto extensions, WASM, plain JS). On hardware with AES-NI/VAES, hardware-accelerated AEGIS or the AEGIS-X modes (see separate entry) are faster than this bitsliced code.
caveats: Published 2026-09, very recent and not yet independently reproduced outside the authors' own two repos. The paper states baselines were 'built and run on the same machines' but does not spell out exact compiler/flags for those builds, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A despite naming every CPU and publishing all code.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=AEGIS: https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1338 'Bitslicing the AEGIS'

name: Rocca (AES-based AEAD for 6G, original/pre-attack version)
workload: Single-thread AEAD encryption throughput at message sizes 64B-16384B on an Intel Core i7-1068NG7, benchmarked against OpenSSL 3.1.0-dev's AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305, plus SNOW-V-GCM and SUPERCOP implementations of AEGIS/Tiaoxin-346.
claimed_speedup: 16384B AEAD: Rocca 150.95 Gbps vs AES-256-GCM 29.08 Gbps (~5.2x) and vs ChaCha20-Poly1305 7.60 Gbps (~19.9x); also stated as 4.16x faster than SNOW-V and 3.10x faster than AES-256-CTR in encryption-only mode
hardware: Intel Core i7-1068NG7 @2.30GHz, 32GB RAM (appendix also reports an Intel Core i9-12900K)
stars_or_usage: Published at a peer-reviewed venue (IACR ePrint 2022/116 / ToSC-adjacent); no widely used reference repo for the original Rocca was located
tradeoffs: The original Rocca was later shown to have practical forgery/committing weaknesses (see IACR ePrint 2024/901 and the ToSC 2024/2025 Derbez et al. and Takeuchi et al. papers) and was superseded by the redesigned Rocca-S. Treat these numbers as a data point on the AES-NI+SIMD 'wide round function' technique, not as a currently-recommended cipher.
caveats: This entry covers the ORIGINAL Rocca design, now considered broken/superseded by Rocca-S; compiler/flags for the OpenSSL comparison are not stated in the paper (hardware is), which caps this at Tier B; no maintained open-source repo of the original Rocca was found in this session (a separate, unrelated Rocca-S implementation exists at jedisct1/zig-rocca-s but was not benchmarked against a named baseline in that repo, so it is not reported as its own entry here).
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=Rocca AES-based encryption beyond 5G: https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/116 'Rocca: An Efficient AES-based Encryption Scheme for Beyond 5G (Full version)'

name: Intel(R) Multi-Buffer Crypto for IPsec (intel-ipsec-mb)
workload: SSE/AVX2/AVX512 multi-buffer job-based AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption, used as a drop-in crypto backend inside DPDK, Intel QAT Engine, and FD.io in place of the default OpenSSL provider

name: blake2_simd (blake2b_simd / blake2s_simd)
workload: Long in-memory inputs hashed with various hash functions (BLAKE3, blake2s_simd, blake2b_simd variants, libsodium BLAKE2b, OpenSSL SHA-1/SHA-512), median cycles-per-byte reported by the bench_multiprocess sub-crate averaging over many runs.

Also beats libsodium's own BLAKE2b (3.07 cpb) by a smaller margin.

Single-machine, single-run-class result (Tier A on methodology completeness, not independently reproduced elsewhere).

name: BLAKE3
baseline: OpenSSL SHA-256, OpenSSL SHA3-256, BLAKE2b, BLAKE2s
workload: Hashing a 16 KiB buffer, single-threaded, via `cargo bench '16384$'`, comparing BLAKE3 against OpenSSL-backed MD5/SHA-1/SHA-2/SHA-3 and the blake2b_simd/blake2s_simd crates
claimed_speedup: 6866 MB/s for BLAKE3 vs 484 MB/s OpenSSL SHA-256 (~14.2x), 394 MB/s OpenSSL SHA3-256 (~17.4x), 1312 MB/s BLAKE2b (~5.2x), 876 MB/s BLAKE2s (~7.8x) (derived from page data)

name: sha2-with-c-intrinsic (AWS Crypto Algorithms Group)
baseline: OpenSSL SHA-256/SHA-512 (SHA Extensions assembly path, commit 13c5d744)
workload: SHA-256 and SHA-512 compression benchmarked on message sizes from 1 to 65536 bytes, isolated per function, 25 warm-up + 100 timed iterations averaged, min of 10 repeats reported, in raw CPU cycles.
claimed_speedup: SHA-256 w/ Intel SHA Extensions, 65536-byte input: 183,685 cycles (their C intrinsics) vs 198,528 cycles (OpenSSL SHA-NI asm) = ~1.08x faster (derived from page data). Their generic/AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 C paths are NOT faster than OpenSSL's corresponding avx/avx2 asm paths on the same table (e.g. avx2 (C) 709,146 cycles vs avx2 (ossl) 620,729 cycles at 65536 bytes -- OpenSSL wins there).
compiler_and_flags: clang-9, -O2/Release (CMake Release build); repo also built/tested with gcc-9
hardware: Dell XPS 13 7390 2-in-1, Intel Core i7-1065G7 (Ice Lake), Turbo Boost off, Ubuntu 18.04.2 LTS
tradeoffs: Provides only raw compression functions (no padding/state management, no shared/static lib); explicitly a benchmarking/compiler-research sample, not intended for production use. Requires SHA_NI/AVX/AVX2/AVX512 capable CPU and matching compiler intrinsics support.
caveats: Mixed result: only the SHA-Extensions code path beats OpenSSL (~8% at large inputs); the plain AVX/AVX2 C intrinsics paths are slower than OpenSSL's own AVX/AVX2 asm on the same benchmark table. Numbers are from 2020 against an OpenSSL dev commit, not a released OpenSSL version; repo has had no commits since 2020 (abandoned). Author affiliation (AWS Crypto Algorithms Group / Gueron & Drucker) lends credibility despite inactivity.

name: j-lanes tree hashing mode and j-lanes SHA-256 (Gueron)
workload: SHA-256 hashing of single messages ranging 2KB-132KB, using a 4-lanes SIMD tree-hashing mode (j=4) on AVX, versus standard serial SHA-256
claimed_speedup: ~2x to ~2.53x faster than OpenSSL 1.0.1c; 1.5x-1.97x faster than the fastest publicly available SHA-256 implementation known to the authors; also faster than tree-mode BLAKE and Keccak (SHA-3 finalists)
hardware: 3rd Generation Intel Core processor (Ivy Bridge, AVX)
tradeoffs: Requires restructuring hashing into a tree mode (message split into j independent SIMD lanes, then combined), which changes the digest unless both hasher and verifier use the same mode; needs AVX; author was an Intel researcher and later pushed related multi-buffer techniques toward OpenSSL/ISA-L.
caveats: IACR ePrint preprint; no compiler or compile flags stated; no public benchmark code linked from the paper; hardware and OpenSSL version (2012-era Ivy Bridge, OpenSSL 1.0.1c) are now over a decade old, so absolute margins on modern OpenSSL (with its own AVX2/SHA-NI paths) are likely smaller.

name: LSH-512
workload: eBACS/SUPERCOP long-message hashing throughput (median of many runs, computed from 1536/4096/18208-byte message timings) on an amd64 test machine
claimed_speedup: ~1.6x faster than BLAKE2b (2.14 vs 3.36 cycles/byte) and ~5.3x faster than SHA3-512 (2.14 vs 11.25 cycles/byte) on long messages (derived from page data)
hardware: amd64-alder eBACS test machine: 2022 Intel Core i3-12100 (Golden Cove, model 90675-00), 4x3300MHz, supercop-20260831
tradeoffs: LSH uses a wider 128-byte block and a generalized-Feistel structure unrelated to Merkle-Damgard SHA-2 or sponge-based SHA-3/BLAKE2; far fewer independent implementations, audits, and years of cryptanalysis than SHA-2/SHA-3/BLAKE2. Only actively-maintained C/C++ library implementation found is Crypto++ (SSE2/AVX2 code, header cites Korea Internet & Security Agency spec).
caveats: The eBACS/SUPERCOP cycles-per-byte numbers are from SUPERCOP's own bundled LSH implementation (submitted by/derived from the KISA designers), not confirmed to be byte-identical to Crypto++'s AVX2 code, though Crypto++ is cited here as the actively-maintained, permissively-licensed C++ implementation of the same standardized algorithm (LSH-512, Korean standard KS X 3262, also ISO/IEC 10118-3:2018). Compiler and flags used per-implementation are not shown on the results page, so tier is capped at B rather than A. Academic cryptanalysis exists on step-reduced/free-start variants of LSH (e.g. IACR eprint 2015/494, later withdrawn); no practical break of full-round LSH-512 is known. Crypto++'s license is public-domain per its own License.txt (compilation copyright only), not a formal SPDX id; treat as no-patent-grant public domain.

name: Simultaneous hashing of multiple messages / S-HASH (Gueron & Krasnov)
workload: 4-buffer parallel (multi-buffer) SHA-256 hashing of multiple independent messages, measured from CPU cache/memory and from disk
claimed_speedup: 3.42x faster than OpenSSL 1.0.1 hashing from cache/memory (5.2 cycles/byte); ~3x faster than OpenSSL 1.0.1 hashing from disk (6.73 cycles/byte); 2.25x faster than the contemporary n-SMS method
hardware: 2nd Generation Intel Core i5-2500 (Sandy Bridge)
tradeoffs: Only pays off when multiple independent messages/buffers can be hashed concurrently (e.g. boot-time integrity checks, multi-stream server workloads); unlike j-lanes (2012/476), gives no benefit for a single serial message.
caveats: IACR ePrint preprint; no compiler/flags stated; 2012-era hardware and OpenSSL 1.0.1; paper mentions the technique was proposed as an OpenSSL patch (RT ticket 2784) but does not confirm it was merged.
found_via: IACR ePrint site search "SHA-256 SIMD faster" -> https://eprint.iacr.org/2012/371, opened and read PDF via curl+pdftotext

name: Intel ISA-L Crypto (multi-buffer SHA)
workload: Multi-buffer hashing: running several independent SHA jobs together on one core via SIMD lane interleaving ("Multi-Hash"), versus single-buffer serial SHA-256 on the same core

baseline: OpenSSL SHA3-256/SHAKE128/SHAKE256 (FIPS 202); OpenSSL SHA-256/SHA-512 (ARM hardware comparison)

claimed_speedup: ~1.18x faster full-session throughput than LibOQS 0.16.0 (13.7-14.1us vs 16.19us total time; ~72,000 vs 61,800 sessions/sec) and faster in all three phases (keygen 4.07 vs 4.72us, encaps 3.84 vs 5.25us, decaps 5.80 vs 6.22us); 2.96x vs Kyber C reference at 47.87us (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: moduletto: rustc, Criterion 0.7, `examples/kyber_benchmark` release build; LibOQS: `cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DOQS_MINIMAL_BUILD=KEM_ml_kem_512 -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-O3 -march=native"` built from tag 0.16.0
hardware: Apple M5 (Mac17,2), macOS Darwin 25.5.0
tradeoffs: NEON-only fast path (i64 NTT + SHA3/inline-Keccak backends are 2.5-3x slower fallbacks for non-ARM); single-developer project, no independent security review; author's own doc flags that fixing FIPS 203 conformance bugs (found via ACVP vectors) was what got it under LibOQS, not the SIMD work alone
caveats: Margin over LibOQS is small (1.18x) and the author explicitly notes LibOQS 0.16.0 is itself 1.26x faster than 0.15.0, so comparisons against older LibOQS releases overstate the lead; the Kyber-C-reference column was carried over from an earlier session and not re-measured in this run; license is PolyForm Noncommercial (non-OSI), so it is usable for study/evaluation but not for commercial redistribution without a separate license
found_via: GitHub code search: "vs liboqs" -> crabnebula-dev/moduletto BENCHMARKS.md

name: sntrup (Streamlined NTRU Prime, pure Rust)
baseline: liboqs (sntrup761, AVX2-dispatched SUPERCOP backend on x86_64 / portable C on aarch64) and PQClean sntrup761 C reference
workload: sntrup761 keypair generation, encapsulation and decapsulation, Criterion benchmarks run in the same process against liboqs (oqs-sys) and PQClean (pqcrypto-ntruprime) in benches/comparison
claimed_speedup: On aarch64 (Apple M2 Max, both refs' portable/NEON-less C paths): keypair 25% faster (1.341ms vs 1.780/1.827ms), encapsulate ~3% faster (50.00us vs 51.54/51.39us), decapsulate ~6% faster (84.52us vs 90.20/90.54us) than both PQClean and liboqs. On x86_64 (Zen 5) it beats PQClean's C reference by 10.0x/7.3x/11.6x on the three operations, but liboqs's AVX2/SUPERCOP kernel still wins there by 3.3x/2.8x/6.3x
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.97.1 (aarch64 run) / rustc 1.98.0-nightly (x86_64 run), cargo release profile, default features except pqcrypto-ntruprime's avx2 feature left off; oqs-sys built from vendored liboqs source
hardware: Apple M2 Max, macOS (aarch64); AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 'Strix Point' Zen 5, Fedora Linux, pinned to one 5.16GHz core via taskset (x86_64)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust with automatic AVX-512/AVX2/AVX-VNNI/NEON runtime dispatch; on x86_64 it does not beat liboqs's hand-tuned AVX2 SUPERCOP kernel, only PQClean's plain C; every secret-derived buffer is zeroized (a security win over the C references, which don't wipe), at a measured ~11% throughput cost that is included in the reported numbers
caveats: The 'beats liboqs' framing only holds on aarch64, where liboqs has no NEON-specific sntrup761 path and falls back to portable C; on x86_64, where liboqs dispatches to its optimized AVX2 code, liboqs remains 2.8x-6.3x faster than this crate for sntrup761. Zero GitHub stars and a single maintainer, but the repo's RESULTS.md is an unusually rigorous same-run engineering log with stated compiler, flags and CPU model for every figure
found_via: GitHub code search: "faster than PQClean" -> mikelodder7/sntrup CHANGELOG.md and benches/comparison/RESULTS.md

name: UltrafastSecp256k1
baseline: OpenSSL (ECDSA_do_sign/ECDSA_do_verify, secp256k1); also benchmarked against libsecp256k1 (bitcoin-core)
workload: Single-operation ECDSA sign/verify and Schnorr (BIP-340) sign/verify on secp256k1, via the project's bench_unified microbenchmark (RDTSCP timer, 11 passes, 500-iteration warmup, pinned core, turbo disabled)
claimed_speedup: ECDSA sign 21.56x, ECDSA verify 10.89x faster than OpenSSL (FAST path; CT-vs-CT signing ~21.7x). Vs libsecp256k1: ECDSA sign ~1.51x, Schnorr sign ~1.48x faster (CT-vs-CT, computed from raw ns: 19441.6 vs 29406.82). On the realistic Bitcoin Core ConnectBlock block-validation workload the margin over libsecp256k1 shrinks to +0.9-1.5% with LTO and -0.5 to -1.0% without LTO
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2.0, Release+LTO, -O3 -flto -march=native (libsecp256k1 comparison compiled -O3 -march=native, no LTO, in the same binary)
hardware: Intel Core i5-14400F; governor=performance, intel_pstate/no_turbo=1, pinned to core 0 via taskset, TSC 2.496GHz
stars_or_usage: 55 stars; proposed (not yet merged) as an opt-in secondary CPU backend for Bitcoin Core
tradeoffs: The large margin over OpenSSL mostly reflects OpenSSL's unoptimized generic EC code path for secp256k1 (a curve OpenSSL does not special-case the way it does NIST P-curves), so it is a much easier target than the curve's actual production incumbent, libsecp256k1; against libsecp256k1 the realistic block-validation workload shows near-parity
caveats: First-party, self-reported benchmark (not independently reproduced by a third party); the repo's own metadata notes a prior benchmark file mislabeled the libsecp256k1 version, later corrected in this file; no external security audit has been performed (all audit evidence is self-generated); the repository's extremely elaborate self-audit/documentation apparatus warrants independent verification of the >10x OpenSSL figures before relying on them

name: VecFalcon (Vectorized Falcon-Sign)
baseline: C-FN-DSA reference implementation (Falcon post-quantum signature reference, github.com/pornin/c-fn-dsa)
workload: Falcon-512 sign_core (vectorized BaseSampler + FFT/iFFT) CPU-cycle benchmark across SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512F, NEON, RV64GC, RV64GCB, RV64GCV, RV64GCVB
claimed_speedup: 13% (SSE2), 23% (AVX2), 36% (AVX-512F), 17% (NEON), 37% (RV64GC), 36% (RV64GCB), 58% (RV64GCV), 59% (RV64GCVB) faster Falcon-512 signature generation vs the C-FN-DSA reference; the vectorized BaseSampler alone is up to 8.4x faster than prior work; RVV FFT/iFFT is 4.1-4.7x faster
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (x86-64, Ubuntu 24.04); Clang 10.0.0 (ARM, Ubuntu 20.04); GCC 13.2.0 (RISC-V, Bianbu 1.0.15)
hardware: Intel i7-11700K (Rocket Lake, 3.6GHz, Turbo Boost and Hyper-Threading disabled); ARM Cortex-A72 (Raspberry Pi 4B, 1.5GHz); SpacemiT X60, RVV v1.0 VLEN=256 (Milk-V Jupiter, 2.0GHz)
stars_or_usage: 4 stars; IACR TCHES 2026 accepted paper artifact
tradeoffs: Baseline is the C-FN-DSA reference implementation, not liboqs's own bundled Falcon backend directly, though the two are architecturally related (liboqs's Falcon derives from the same lineage of reference/optimized code); the vectorized BaseSampler deliberately breaks bit-for-bit KAT reproducibility with official test vectors while preserving verification interoperability
caveats: Comparison baseline (C-FN-DSA) is a reference/portable implementation rather than the most heavily optimized prior Falcon code; percentages quoted are for signature generation only (not keygen or verify); GitHub's license detector reports NOASSERTION even though the LICENSE file and paper both state MIT

name: Code Generation of Faster Formally Verified NTT with Plantard Reduction
baseline: liboqs ML-KEM/ML-DSA NIST PQC reference C implementations (mlkem-native / mldsa-native)
workload: ML-KEM-512 decapsulation/encapsulation/keygen and ML-DSA-2 signing/verification/keygen CPU cycle counts; also isolated forward/inverse NTT cycle counts
claimed_speedup: End-to-end vs NIST PQC reference C: ML-KEM-512 decap +1.32x, encap +1.27x, keygen +1.17x; ML-DSA-2 sign +1.26x, verify +1.16x, keygen +1.11x; NTT-only 1.5x-1.8x forward, 1.7x-2.5x inverse; also 1.26x/2.19x over the formally verified formosa-mlkem Jasmin baseline on ML-KEM
compiler_and_flags: gcc-11.4 -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer (C path); Jasmin 2025.6.1 + clang-14 -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer (verified backend)
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2314 @ 2.80GHz, 4 cores, TurboBoost/Hyper-Threading disabled
tradeoffs: Improves only the NTT component, not a full drop-in library; targets ML-KEM/ML-DSA/FN-DSA jointly from one code generator, so gains are shared but modest end-to-end (<1.3x for most operations).
caveats: 2026 preprint (IACR ePrint marks it 'Preprint', not peer-reviewed); paper states code is available at an anonymous.4open.science double-blind-review link, but that URL returned HTTP 401 when I checked it this session, so the repository could not be independently opened -- capped below Tier A on that basis even though CPU, compiler and methodology are fully stated in the PDF I did open.

name: GOLF: GPU-accelerated Optimization for Lattice-based FALCON
baseline: FALCON reference implementation (the portable C backend bundled in liboqs)
workload: FALCON signature generation/verification throughput (ops/sec) on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 vs the single-core reference FALCON implementation
claimed_speedup: 42.02 kops/s signing, 10,311.04 kops/s verification on RTX 4090; 58.05x sign / 73.14x verify over the reference FALCON implementation; 7.17x/3.79x over the fastest prior GPU implementation
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (GPU side only); CPU model for the reference baseline is not stated in the abstract/page text I could access
tradeoffs: No public code repository located; batched GPU throughput number, not single-operation latency; needs large batches and a CUDA GPU to realize the claimed gains.
caveats: IACR ePrint marks this a 'Preprint' (not peer-reviewed); no code found via GitHub search; CPU baseline hardware and compiler flags not confirmed from the accessible page, and the >50x ratio with unstated baseline build flags means this is capped at Tier C per the implausible-ratio rule.
